articles.title: Boluda Towage opens new Antwerp headquarters
articles.summary: Boluda Towage has inaugurated its new headquarters at Noorderplaats in Antwerp, strengthening its operational base in Belgium and the wider Scheldt region. articles.body: Boluda Towage has inaugurated its new headquarters at Noorderplaats in Antwerp, strengthening its operational base in Belgium and the wider Scheldt region. The facility includes modern office space and a dedicated training simulator designed to support crew development and the onboarding of new employees. Steven De Nijs, Deputy CEO of Boluda Towage Europe, and Filip De Wilde, the newly appointed General Manager of Boluda Towage in Belgium, led the inauguration. Representatives of port authorities, customers, employees and business partners also attended the event. Boluda Towage has operated in Antwerp since 2019, while its Belgian maritime operations trace their history back to 1870. Simulator supports crew training The simulator will form part of Boluda Towage’s training programme for crews and tug captains. It will allow personnel to practise vessel handling and manoeuvring under realistic operating conditions. The training will also focus on decision-making, situational awareness, communication and preparation for different port scenarios within a controlled environment. Experienced captains who remain involved in daily towage operations will deliver the simulator-based training, bringing practical operational knowledge into the development programme. The facility is intended to support Boluda Towage Antwerp as the company expands its operations across the Scheldt region. Northern Europe represents a significant market for the towage operator. Boluda Towage currently operates in more than 21 ports across the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium, Finland and Norway, with a regional fleet of 138 vessels. The Antwerp opening follows the inauguration of Boluda Towage’s Rotterdam headquarters in July 2026. The two facilities form part of the company’s wider strategy to strengthen its European network and develop local maritime expertise.

Rozema Boat Works, Inc. , of Mount Vernon, Washington, won a contract for the construction of a 56-ft. pilot transfer vessel for the Tampa Bay Pilots Association , based in Tampa Bay, Florida. Designed by Camarc Design , the all-aluminum vessel features a refined double-chine hull optimized for efficient, reliable performance and safe pilot transfer operations in a wide range of operating conditions. The vessel will be powered by twin Caterpillar C-18 diesel engines rated at 715 horsepower at 2100rpm. The vessel will be equipped with conventional propellers, delivering a top speed of approximately 27-28 knots. The propulsion and control systems are configured to provide responsive handling and maneuverability, supporting safe operations alongside commercial vessels. Configured to carry up to five pilots in addition to crew, the vessel incorporates a practical layout with heavy-duty fendering and a rescue platform to support day-to-day pilot transfer and recovery operations. The onboard systems package includes modern Furuno navigation electronics suite, climate-controlled accommodations, and equipment suited for continuous commercial service. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS Conflicting traffic figures and competing claims of control are making it increasingly difficult to establish what’s happening in the Strait of Hormuz, even as attacks on merchant shipping intensify. The true extent of attacks on merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz remains unclear, with a new report from UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) acknowledging that most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents directly to the maritime security organization. The admission comes as the United States and Iran offer sharply different accounts of who controls the vital waterway, while conflicting transit figures raise further questions about how much commercial shipping has actually recovered. In its weekly overview published Friday , UKMTO said it is struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted are refusing to submit reports. UKMTO said it is aware of additional incidents through other sources but cannot include them in its reporting without sufficient verification. The disclosure raises questions about the reliability of publicly available attack statistics, particularly following a sharp escalation in strikes against commercial vessels over the past two weeks. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during its latest reporting period, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Six vessels continued their voyages or reached port, two were disabled or left not under command, and three had unconfirmed damage or outcomes. One vessel, the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride , was lost after being struck by a projectile. The report also found that 55 of 74 documented projectile strikes since July 6 occurred along the southern route through the strait, accounting for nearly three-quarters of the reported attacks. The findings stand in contrast to increasingly confident statements from U.S. military officials about their control of the waterway. In a video statement Friday, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, said American forces and regional partners remain firmly in control of the strait despite continued Iranian attacks. “Let me be clear: the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran. And it remains open for business,” Cooper said. He reported that approximately 400 merchant ships had transited the strait over the preceding seven days, while U.S. forces helped Gulf partners move more than 100 million barrels of crude oil during the same period. Cooper said those shipments added to more than 1.3 billion barrels of crude transported with U.S. assistance in recent months. But the latest UKMTO figures paint a different picture. For the seven days ending October 14, UKMTO recorded 254 combined transits, including 129 inbound and 125 outbound movements. That was down from 275 the previous week, with traffic remaining approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Of those 254 movements, just 42 were observed through Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. The remaining 212 were drawn from U.S.-reported facilitated transits, which include ships operating without broadcasting AIS. UKMTO cautioned that the U.S.-supplied figures and associated totals cannot currently be independently verified. Cooper did not specify the exact dates covered by his 400-transit figure, leaving open the possibility that the difference reflects separate reporting periods or counting methods. Nevertheless, the gap illustrates the difficulty of establishing a consistent picture of commercial traffic through the strait. Iran, meanwhile, continues to dispute Washington’s account of control over the waterway. Iranian army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said Thursday that the strait would remain closed until the rights of the Iranian people were respected. The latest Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) advisory , published October 15, describes both a northern Iranian-controlled route and a southern Omani corridor, while warning that ships operating with AIS switched on face an elevated risk of targeting and instructions to divert toward the Iranian route. UKMTO’s latest report adds that most vessels broadcasting AIS continue to use the Iranian route, even as U.S.-facilitated traffic accounts for the majority of reported transits. The competing accounts reflect the increasingly complicated security environment for merchant shipping. U.S. forces are facilitating substantial traffic through the strait, while Iran continues to demonstrate an ability to strike vessels, including those using the southern corridor. And with UKMTO now acknowledging that most attacked vessels are not reporting incidents directly, even the growing number of documented strikes may offer only a partial picture of the dangers facing seafarers. articles.title: Fincantieri Integrates AI, Robotics to Advance Shipyards
articles.summary: Fincantieri is accelerating the transformation of its shipyards through the integration of advanced robotics, Physical AI, and next-generation automation systems, with the aim of making production processes increasingly efficient, safe, and…
articles.body: Fincantieri Integrates AI, Robotics to Advance Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Fincantieri Fincantieri is accelerating the transformation of its shipyards through the integration of advanced robotics, Physical AI, and next-generation automation systems, with the aim of making production processes increasingly efficient, safe, and competitive. This is the vision behind BOOST² – The Shipyard of the Future, the industrial innovation program launched by the Group three years ago to identify, develop, and integrate new technologies into its production processes. Throughout its journey, the initiative has engaged more than 450 Fincantieri employees across 13 shipyards in Italy and abroad, including facilities in Romania and the United States, fostering direct interaction with operational needs and actively involving people in the development of new solutions. As part of the Industrial Plan, the program provides for investments of almost 100 million euros. The program’s latest achievements were presented at the Castellammare di Stabia shipyard through demonstrations of solutions already in operation, technologies currently undergoing validation, and applications destined for further evolution. Following an initial phase focused on technology scouting and experimentation, the program is now geared towards accelerating the transition from innovation to industrial deployment, supporting the adoption of new solutions in day-to-day operations and their progressive rollout across the Group’s shipyards. This approach builds on the results achieved so far and aims to further strengthen the integration of technologies, industrial expertise, and the practical needs of production. In this context, collaboration with the innovation ecosystem plays a key role. Through its Open Innovation strategy, Fincantieri identifies and selects technology partners in Italy and internationally, including SMEs and start-ups, to develop and tailor solutions to the specific needs of the shipbuilding industry. The direct involvement of people and production teams is an integral part of the process, enabling field testing, accelerating adoption, and ensuring that technologies can be scaled and replicated across different manufacturing environments. At the heart of the program are Physical AI, which enables intelligent systems to interact with the physical world, and collaborative robotics, with applications designed to support people in carrying out the most complex tasks. These technologies are complemented by Digital Twin solutions for the digital management of shipyard assets and processes, Smart Supply Chain systems, additive manufacturing, and automated solutions for industrial equipment. The objective is to unlock the full potential of these technologies by progressively integrating them into operational workflows and strengthening the connection between design, planning, and production.

articles.body: Oil Prices Rise by More Than 3% Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Adobe Stock/hunterpic2013 Oil prices gained more than 3% and were heading for weekly gains on continued uncertainty over Middle East supplies, and as investors kept assessing how much diesel Russia could supply to the global markets. Brent crude futures were up $3.41, or 3.2%, at $109.34 at 12:41 p.m. ET (1641 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose $2.74, or 2.8%, to $100.67, crossing $100 for the first time since September 21. So far this week, Brent has risen 4.1% and WTI 8.6%. "Conflict in the Middle East still keeps coming back and I think it's questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets. Those two factors are just continuing to have traders be buyers," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial. Supply concerns also increased as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. Yemen's Houthis also fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people. "Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower," Kpler analysts said in a report on Thursday, adding that they expected a slower and more uneven recovery in Hormuz flows in the absence of a comprehensive political deal. Meanwhile, Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump and criticised Trump's willingness to strike deals with Moscow. Russia's Ryazan oil refinery has suspended operations at a primary crude distillation unit following a drone attack in the region on Thursday, two industry sources told Reuters. The IEA agreed on Thursday to release more than 20 million barrels of fuel to the market. Those margins rose as high as $95 a barrel in September as diesel supply tightened because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Brent crude was little changed on Thursday, while WTI settled up more than 3% after news that the US was weighing plans to ease restrictions on the world’s "shadow fleet" of tankers and after a big US crude stock draw on hurricane production shut-ins. (Reuters)

articles.title: BPA analysis attributes UK container growth to port investment
articles.summary: New analysis from the British Ports Association challenges claims that EU Emissions Trading System pricing is diverting container traffic from continental Europe to Britain, finding instead that infrastructure investment is the primary driver of growing UK port competitiveness. The EU earlier this year proposed...
articles.body: New analysis from the British Ports Association challenges claims that EU Emissions Trading System pricing is diverting container traffic from continental Europe to Britain, finding instead that infrastructure investment is the primary driver of growing UK port competitiveness. The EU earlier this year proposed measures to penalise UK container ports based on reports from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory suggesting that a sharp increase in the UK’s share of Northern European container shipping activity constituted evidence of carbon leakage. The BPA analysis disputes this conclusion, finding that the figures do not reflect actual changes in cargo volumes and overlook major port investments and changes in global shipping networks. The analysis notes that UK container volume growth in 2025 was concentrated in approximately 85% in London, following the opening of a new GBP 350 million berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Concurrently, major continental ports including Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg also recorded growth during the same period, undermining the carbon leakage thesis. Mark Simmonds, Director of Policy and External Affairs at the British Ports Association, stated that British ports have invested hundreds of millions of pounds to attract more ships and handle more cargo, and that those investments are delivering results through improved competitiveness. He described it as extraordinary that the EU might respond to that success by introducing measures to penalise British ports, arguing that all available evidence, including the EU’s own assessments and data, shows that UK throughput increases align with new port capacity coming online. While expressing support for efforts to reduce shipping emissions, he emphasised that climate policy must be based on sound evidence rather than assumptions that could damage competition and investment.

Stock Photo: Nickeo23/Shutterstock Deal adds four modern crude tankers as International Seaways reports sharply higher spot earnings entering the fourth quarter. International Seaways has agreed to acquire Oslo-listed Bruton Limited in a deal valued at approximately $370 million, adding four very large crude carriers (VLCCs) to its fleet as tanker earnings remain elevated. The New York-based tanker owner announced the agreement Friday, saying the acquisition will expand its fleet of approximately 70 crude oil and product tankers. The deal includes one VLCC already in operation and three newbuildings under construction at China’s New Times Shipyard. The acquisition comes alongside preliminary financial results showing strong tanker market conditions. International Seaways reported average blended spot earnings of approximately $68,000 per day during the third quarter, more than double the $29,000 per day recorded a year earlier. Rates have climbed further entering the fourth quarter. The company said it has secured blended spot earnings averaging approximately $180,000 per day for about 37% of its expected fourth-quarter revenue days. Under the acquisition agreement, International Seaways will initially acquire a 50.5% stake in Bruton through a share exchange with existing shareholders, expected to settle around October 20. The company will then acquire the remaining shares through a cash-and-stock merger. International Seaways expects to issue approximately 3.12 million shares as part of the transaction, accounting for roughly 96% of the total consideration. The remainder will be paid in cash. Bruton shareholders are scheduled to vote on the merger around October 30, with the transaction expected to close shortly afterward, subject to customary conditions. “We’re excited about the opportunity to expand and modernize our fleet through this accretive transaction with Bruton,” said Lois K. Zabrocky, president and CEO of International Seaways. “The transaction underscores our disciplined approach to growth.” Bruton’s fleet consists of the 300,000-dwt Mount Vision, delivered in July, and three sister vessels scheduled for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027. According to Bruton’s fleet information, Mount Vision is earning $95,000 per day under its existing charter, while the next vessel, Mount Horizon, has secured a charter at $105,700 per day. Bruton previously controlled a larger VLCC newbuilding program, but spun off eight vessels into OMC Tankers, which began trading in Oslo in August. Those eight newbuildings are not part of the International Seaways acquisition. International Seaways also expects third-quarter revenue of $480 million to $490 million and net income of $340 million to $350 million, including an approximately $50 million gain from the sale of a 2012-built Suezmax tanker. The company reported liquidity of approximately $965 million at September 30, including $455 million in cash and short-term investments. Its full third-quarter financial results are scheduled for release on November 5. articles.summary: The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September, handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September, handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting global trade patterns continued to drive cargo through the nation’s busiest port complex. The Port of Long Beach reported Thursday that it handled 997,177 TEUs in September, up 25% from a year earlier and surpassing its previous record of 987,191 TEUs set in October 2024. It was the busiest month in the port’s 115-year history. The milestone follows last week’s record-breaking announcement from the Port of Los Angeles , which handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September, the highest monthly total in its 118-year history. Together, the neighboring ports moved 2,039,829 TEUs in September, including more than 1.05 million TEUs of loaded imports, as retailers continued replenishing inventories and shippers adjusted their routing strategies amid high fuel costs, trade uncertainty and disruptions along other major shipping routes. “Shippers continue to lean on the Port of Long Beach as a reliable partner in their business strategies, leading to our historic month for cargo,” said Port of Long Beach CEO Noel Hacegaba during the port’s monthly Supply Chain Insight briefing. Imports led the surge at Long Beach, climbing 31.3% from a year earlier to 509,390 TEUs. Exports increased 7.8% to 91,747 TEUs, while empty container movements rose 22.1% to 396,040 TEUs. Los Angeles reported similarly strong numbers, with loaded imports rising 19% to 545,696 TEUs. The port also handled 125,751 TEUs of exports and approximately 371,206 empty TEUs, both increases from a year earlier. Port officials have attributed the strong performance to several factors, including resilient consumer demand, lower U.S. tariffs and shippers seeking alternatives to traditional routes affected by Panama Canal restrictions and security concerns around the Suez Canal. High diesel prices have also made the shorter transpacific route to the U.S. West Coast more attractive. The record-breaking September comes as the National Retail Federation (NRF) expects the unusually long peak shipping season to finally wind down. In its latest Global Port Tracker report , released October 8, NRF and Hackett Associates projected that imports at major U.S. container ports would ease from 2.3 million TEUs in August to 2.28 million TEUs in September, followed by 2.25 million TEUs in October and 2 million TEUs in November. “Even with any fluctuations in final data, we’re likely past the busiest part of the year,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF vice president for supply chain and customs policy. The forecast follows months of stronger-than-expected imports that extended the traditional peak season well into the fall. Notably, both Southern California ports have reported handling the increased volumes without the congestion that disrupted operations during the pandemic. At Long Beach, Total Terminals International set a new monthly rail record in September, handling 59,410 rail moves, representing nearly half of the terminal’s container volume. Long Beach has now handled 7,675,255 TEUs through the first nine months of 2026, up 3.9% from the same period last year. Los Angeles has processed nearly 8.1 million TEUs over the same period, more than 3% ahead of last year’s pace. articles.summary: The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are demonstrating the limits of the kingdom’s military prowess — despite defense spending that far outstrips that of its regional neighbors.

REUTERS/Khaled Abdullah By Gerry Doyle (Bloomberg) — The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are demonstrating the limits of the kingdom’s military prowess — despite defense spending that far outstrips that of its regional neighbors. Missiles and drones fired by the Iran-backed group from Yemen have wreaked havoc in Saudi Arabia in recent days, killing at least 18 people and forcing the closure of the country’s main international airport in Riyadh. The Houthis are showing no sign of scaling back their campaign, targeting several Saudi Arabian cities in an assault this week that’s continued into Thursday. Saudi Arabia allocated between $64 billion and $96 billion this year for defense, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Economics. The upper end is more than twice as much as Israel, the next biggest Middle East spender. The kingdom operates Raytheon Co. Patriot missile batteries with the latest Lockheed Martin Corp. PAC-3 interceptors, flies hundreds of Boeing Co. F-15 fighters customized for its air force, and is the only Gulf country with mid-air refueling aircraft. One reason the Houthis have been able to cause such destruction with less advanced equipment is Saudi Arabia’s size, which complicates defense efforts. The kingdom covers more than 2.1 million square kilometers (830,000 square miles), with many strategic targets to protect, from oil infrastructure to air bases to several large cities. Defending against ballistic missiles is complex when protecting a single target, let alone sites sprinkled across a vast country. Thousands of Iranian strikes across the Arabian peninsula during the initial phase of the US and Israeli war on the Islamic Republic were largely thwarted by missile defenses, but even a 90% success rate can mean massive damage on the ground. Saudi Arabia’s military is also still in the process of modernizing and remains heavily reliant on the US for military intelligence. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment. The most recent rounds of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have tended to involve a mix of weapons that further complicate defensive efforts: small drones, low-flying, cheap cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. In addition, the Houthis are a nimble, rapidly evolving opponent backed by Iran, capable of building and deploying missiles and drones that can challenge even advanced defense systems. Years of fighting in Yemen mean the group is battle hardened, resisting protracted military efforts to dislodge or contain them. “The Houthis are partly beneficiaries of good fortune, but they seem remarkably adaptive,” said Ankit Panda, Stanton Senior Fellow in the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “A determined attacker armed with missiles is still difficult to deal with.” The Houthi arsenal has now evolved to the point where the group can manufacture relatively precise drones and ballistic missiles — some of which rely on parts from Chinese companies. Those munitions might cost thousands, or hundreds of thousands of dollars, far cheaper than the multimillion-dollar air defense interceptors used to stop them. That means even a successfully intercepted attack imposes further costs on Saudi Arabia, and makes it more vulnerable to future strikes. Defensive weapons such as the Iranian-made 358 surface-to-air missiles — which can loiter at high altitudes and strike subsonic aircraft — make the skies over Yemen dangerous too. Another issue, said Bloomberg Economics defense lead Becca Wasser, is that Patriot air defense batteries are directional. They do not cover a 360-degree area, so if radars and launchers were positioned to intercept Iranian fire, they may not have been able to easily shoot down Houthi missiles, she said. Air and missile capabilities have improved as part of Saudi Arabia’s modernization efforts, Wasser said. Although pilots learned considerably from the long Yemen air war, their aircraft remain largely reliant on the US for targeting data, in particular. The situation has improved since Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman began a reform agenda, alongside “real-life experience in its first war against Yemen,” Wasser said. “But modernization is slow and confined to pockets of bright spots rather than upskilling across the force.” Although Riyadh has a fleet of more than 200 F-15 jets — almost as many as the US Air Force — it was unable to use them decisively in more than a decade of bombing the Houthis. Saudi Arabia went to war with the militant group in 2015 after it took control of the Yemeni capital, Saana, though fighting receded between a 2022 truce and the recent flare up. “Equipment and funding do not win wars,” said Wolf-Christian Paes, a senior fellow for armed conflict at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. “Training, motivation and leadership do.” US influence in the Middle East after 1990 — when Washington intervened after Iraq invaded Kuwait — prompted many countries in the region to rely on US firepower rather than fully develop their own capabilities. Saudi Arabia was not immune to this “protection curse,” said David Roberts, a reader in international security and Middle East studies at King’s College London. US struggles in Afghanistan, and incidents like the 2019 Houthi drone attack against oil facilities in Abqaiq, in the east of Saudi Arabia, punctured the image that “Uncle Sam would basically detect and protect,” Roberts said. US President Donald Trump has so far opted against intervening directly in the current conflict. In a post on Truth Social on Tuesday he said the Houthis were “behaving very badly,” without specifying what action the US could take. Saudi Oil Minister Prince Abdul Aziz Bin Salman said this week that “the events of recent weeks are serious,” adding that the kingdom’s response “must be equally serious, while remaining focused on the decades ahead.” The Houthis began threatening shipping in the Red Sea after the start of the war in Gaza, which prompted the US to briefly intervene, launching more than 1,000 strikes over three months. But hunting down hidden, mobile launchers and shutting down buried production facilities is difficult, especially in the rugged terrain in which the Houthis operate. The operation ended with a ceasefire. The Houthis show “there are very clear limits what an air campaign can do,” said April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Former US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, speaking at the Warsaw Defense Forum on Monday, said Saudi Arabia would most likely need help from friendly nations to counter the Houthi threat. “There will be a concerted effort to get the Houthi thing under control,” he said. “But it won’t be easy. They are much more resilient than most people recognize.” The conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have shown how the power of ballistic missiles, particularly those with a range of 1,000 kilometers or more, mean even countries whose millitaries are relatively weak can cause problems for more powerful adversaries. The Houthis’ strike arsenal includes indigenously produced Quds-1 cruise missiles, which have a reach of about 750 kilometers, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Its homegrown ballistic arsenal is larger, with Burkan-1, -2, and -3 designs, which can fly 600 kilometers, 850 kilometers and 1,200 kilometers, respectively, giving the militants the range to hit nearly any site in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh’s struggles to extinguish the Houthi threat and defend against counterattacks reflects the difficulty of a task many others have failed at too. “Yemen is a hard nut to crack. The US couldn’t do it,” Longley Alley said. “This is something that can’t be solved with a military tool only.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe. The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake,” Dan wrote on X after a meeting with NATO chief Mark Rutte to discuss a recent spate of such attacks. “NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” Rutte said regarding the incident. He said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.” What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea? Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire. Romania’s naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader. This comes as shipping in the Black Sea has come under increasing attacks ⁠in recent months that have drastically reduced grain transports from both Ukraine and Russia, both major cereal exporters. articles.body: Pacific Environment welcomes Singapore grant to accelerate electric harbour craft adoption in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 16/10/2026 On 14 October 2026, The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) announced the Early Adopter Scheme for Electric Harbour Craft (EASE), offering harbour craft operators of up to S$250,000 per vessel to support the transition to electric vessels. By helping to offset upfront costs, the grant aims to catalyse early demand and encourage more operators to make the switch to electric vessels. Early adoption will help to address the chicken-and-egg challenge facing vessel electrification, where limited demand can constrain investment in the technologies and infrastructure needed to achieve scale. The scheme marks a strong policy push by Singapore’s authorities, complementing the requirement for all new harbour craft operating in its waters from 2030 to be fully electric, capable of using B100 biofuel, or compatible with net-zero fuels. Realising the full potential of these incentives will require parallel progress in enabling infrastructure. To this end, Singapore will continue expanding its charging infrastructure, including four additional chargers at Loyang Offshore Supply Base and more public chargers at Jurong Port and West Coast Pier in 2027. “Pacific Environment welcomes the grant and commitment to zero-emissions harbour craft in Singapore’s waters. It sends a clear and strong policy signal that will accelerate market development and spur investment in electric vessels. Singapore has demonstrated leadership through its progressive policies and initiatives to decarbonise its domestic harbour craft sector, and this latest measure further strengthens its position as a frontrunner in maritime electrification.” – Lim Jie Ying, Singapore climate specialist at Pacific Environment. Pacific Environment looks forward to continued collaboration with Singapore’s maritime stakeholders to support the sector’s net-zero goals. Prioritising direct electrification and the development of its supporting infrastructure will be critical to delivering meaningful emissions reductions, alongside genuinely sustainable net-zero fuels where direct electrification is not feasible. Singapore’s experience in developing strong policy frameworks to accelerate maritime decarbonisation offers valuable lessons for ports around the world. articles.body: DP World Deploys 55 Electric Yard Tractors At South Korea’s Busan Terminal in Port News 16/10/2026 DP World has deployed 55 electric yard tractors (E-YTs) at its Busan terminal in South Korea, marking a significant step up in its efforts to reduce emissions from terminal operations. The new E-YTs replace Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG)-powered vehicles and account for approximately 36% of the terminal’s 154-strong yard tractor fleet. Used to move containers across the terminal, the electric tractors are expected to reduce CO₂ emissions by approximately 70% per unit compared with the LNG-powered tractors they replace. The transition to electric equipment will also reduce the use and disposal of engine fluids, helping to minimise the risk of leaks and the environmental impact of terminal operations. As a participant in South Korea’s Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), DP World Busan is taking steps to reduce emissions from its operations. The deployment of E-YTs supports these efforts and is aligned with South Korea’s broader ambitions to advance low-carbon logistics and greener port operations. Anders Dømmestrup, Chief Operating Officer, Ports & Terminals, Asia Pacific, DP World APAC, said: “Deploying these electric yard tractors marks an important milestone in DP World’s efforts to reduce emissions from terminal operations. It shows how we can make progress on that goal while continuing to deliver the safe, efficient and reliable services our customers depend on.” In addition to the environmental benefits, the electric tractors offer quieter operation, smoother acceleration and more consistent performance during frequent stop-and-go movements. With fewer moving parts than LNG-powered tractors, they are also expected to require less maintenance, supporting equipment availability and operational efficiency. DP World Busan plans to continue expanding the use of electric equipment as part of its longer-term efforts to reduce terminal emissions. The deployment builds on similar electrification initiatives across DP World’s global ports and terminals, including the Port of Brisbane on Fisherman Island in Australia, Manila South Harbour in the Philippines and Laem Chabang International Terminal in Thailand. These efforts demonstrate DP World’s sustainability commitment and its broader mission to decarbonise port operations globally. Source: DP World 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: European gas consolidates near 2022 peaks to lock in 3rd weekly gain in General Energy News 16/10/2026 European and British wholesale natural gas futures held largely steady on Friday, hovering near their highest levels since late 2022 to lock in a third consecutive week of gains as structural supply anxieties continued to dominate energy bourses. The steady performance capped a nearly 6% weekly advance for the European benchmark, marking its third straight week of price gains. Ongoing maritime attacks and new targeting tactics near the Strait of Hormuz have constrained seaborne Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) deliveries transiting the Persian Gulf. Extended, costly carrier reroutings around the Cape of Good Hope have delayed spot cargoes bound for European regasification terminals. Unplanned maintenance outages across Norwegian gas infrastructure earlier in the week – including reduced processing capacity at the Kårstø plant – curbed pipeline delivery volumes into Western European hubs, forcing utilities to bid up spot paper. European Union underground gas storage facilities sit at approximately 74% capacity – well below the historical average of roughly 86% typically seen at this point in mid-October. With storage caverns starting from a significantly lower baseline ahead of peak winter drawdown, trading desks warn that any late-October cold snap or further LNG supply disruption could trigger a fresh leg higher across continental gas curves. articles.title: Fed’s Warsh surprised by world economy’s ‘resilience’
articles.summary: US Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said Friday the global economy had shown unexpected resilience against strong economic shocks, as central banks battle surging inflation, while rich countries tackle spiking bond yields. “Almost everywhere in the global economy (is) showing resilience I’m not sure I would have...
articles.body: Fed’s Warsh surprised by world economy’s ‘resilience’ in World Economy News 16/10/2026 US Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said Friday the global economy had shown unexpected resilience against strong economic shocks, as central banks battle surging inflation, while rich countries tackle spiking bond yields. “Almost everywhere in the global economy (is) showing resilience I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago,” he told an event hosted by IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. World energy prices have skyrocketed since US President Donald Trump launched the war on Iran in February, sparking retaliatory action by Tehran against Washington’s Gulf allies and plunging the Middle East into crisis. The increase in oil and gas costs, along with a surge in AI investments, has spurred inflation in many economies, including the United States, putting pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. While many other rich economies were able to bring post-pandemic inflation back to their targets, the Fed has failed to meet its long-term two-percent goal for more than five years. Since taking over as Fed chair in May, Warsh has promised the central bank will deliver on its price stability commitment, and in September it raised rates for the first time in three years. The Fed meets again this month to set rates, and markets expect it to hold before a second 25-basis-point hike in December. Warsh has vowed to cut down on providing insights into Fed policy positions, and on Friday again refrained from sharing his view of what may transpire at the October gathering. “We came to a judgement” about the economic outlook at the September meeting, he said. “I want to say broadly over the month or so that’s transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations.” The annual meetings bring together finance ministers, central bankers and policymakers from around the world, and Warsh said he had heard from others of the “common challenges” advanced economies faced. “I heard, I would say, resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability,” he said. Most rich nations have begun to raise rates in response to surging inflation, including the European Central Bank (ECB). “If I look back over the last few months, while we each did the right thing by our own judgement, by our own remit, it was a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world,” said Warsh. “And that means there’s no free riders. We’re seeing common things, and we’re taking action, and I view that as a positive development.” Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin told AFP on Friday that rising bond yields in his country were effectively helping the ECB to tighten financial conditions. “This tightening of financial conditions, driven by this rise in long-term rates, may provide the ECB with greater flexibility to control inflation,” he said. Earlier this week, ECB chief Christine Lagarde said France would have to address its rising bond yields on the fiscal side and should not expect help from the central bank. A large part of the discussion on Friday centred on AI, and Warsh said he believed the technology was the “most consequential change” to the global economy he had seen, predicting its effects would be positive but the path forward “bumpy”. He said he takes the macroeconomic implications of the technology — including a short-term driving of inflation through demand-side effects and an expected positive supply-side shock in the long term — “soberly” in his role as Fed chief. While he conceded the AI investment boom would drive prices up in the short term, he felt there was a “huge benefit” to the global economy on the horizon. He cautioned, however, that the path forward was still laced with uncertainty about how markets would evolve around the technology. “The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies,” he said. articles.body: OECD employment and labour force participation rates at record highs in Q2 2026; unemployment rate remains near record low in August in IMF/OECD News 16/10/2026 OECD employment and labour force participation rates reached record highs in Q2 2026, at 70.4% and 74.2%, respectively. However, both rates increased by 0.1 percentage point (p.p.) or less from the previous quarter, remaining broadly stable (Figure 1). Compared with the same quarter in 2025, both rates were also broadly unchanged. Employment and labour force participation rates were, respectively, at or near record highs in 9 and 13 OECD countries (Figure 3, Tables 1 and 2). Meanwhile, the OECD unemployment rate was broadly stable in August 2026, at 5.0%, just 0.2 p.p. above its record low from June 2023 (Figure 1, 5 and Table 3). Employment rates across OECD countries ranged from 54.8% in Q2 2026 in Türkiye to above 80% in Iceland, Japan and the Netherlands. The largest year-on-year increases were recorded in Colombia and Portugal, at 1.5 and 1.3 p.p. respectively, reflecting higher labour force participation combined with lower unemployment. Conversely, employment rates fell most in Iceland and Finland, by 3.3 and 1.1 p.p. respectively, mainly reflecting higher unemployment. Smaller declines observed in Israel and Luxembourg were mainly driven by lower labour force participation (Figure 3). Across population groups, women’s employment and labour force participation rates each rose by 0.2 p.p. in Q2 2026, while rates for men remained broadly stable. By age group, the OECD employment and labour force participation rates rose by 0.4 and 0.2 p.p. among older workers aged 55-64 years old, while remaining broadly stable for prime-age workers aged 25-54 and young people aged 15-24 (Figure 2). In August 2026, unemployment rates in 20 OECD countries as well as in the European Union (6.1%) and the euro area (6.4%) remained largely unchanged compared with July. Unemployment rates increased in seven countries, most notably in Colombia, while decreases were observed in Denmark, Finland, Greece, Israel and Türkiye. The OECD unemployment rate among younger workers aged 15-24 rose to 11.3% from 11.0% in July, widening the gap between younger workers and workers aged 25 and over (Figure 5 and Table 6). More timely estimates for September 2026 show that unemployment rates remained broadly stable in Canada and the United States at 6.5% and 4.2%, respectively. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) – The cost ?of shipping oil on the largest tankers fell this week from record highs as demand eased following a wave of attacks on vessels in the Middle East and as the US considered easing sanctions on the so-called shadow fleet. Freight rates ?for supertankers, also known as very large crude carriers (VLCCs), carrying oil ?from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to about 776 ?on the Worldscale basis, according to Baltic Exchange ?data. That was down from 841 last week, the highest since the rate was launched earlier this year, following gains since the outbreak of the Iran war. “Gulf of Oman VLCC rates dropped as demand on that route has softened since the fresh attacks, as higher Middle East Gulf freight rates and subsequently lower export volumes have reduced demand on this route,” said Kpler analyst Matthew Wright. Trump administration comments about potentially removing sanctions on some shadow-fleet tankers drove freight rates lower, Sparta Commodities analyst Michael Ryan said, adding a removal would increase the number of ships that can carry oil. Despite the drop, rates remain close to record highs. The US-Israeli war on Iran has increased the use of ship-to-ship transfers to move oil out of the Strait of Hormuz, boosting demand for tankers. If elevated shipping costs persist, they could add to inflationary pressures and raise costs for businesses and consumers. Rates have also eased from record highs on other routes this week, such as from West Africa to Asia. (Reporting by Enes Tunagur in London. articles.body: Rhenus is expanding its logistics operations in Italy with a new 10,000 sqm hub at Interporto Padova. The facility will bring together transport, warehousing and freight forwarding services in one location. The company plans to begin moving operations to the new site in the first quarter of 2027. The move will double its covered logistics space in the Padua area from approximately 5,000 sqm to 10,000 sqm. The new hub will combine activities currently handled at two nearby warehouses. It will also increase Rhenus’ capacity to manage domestic and international freight. Bringing logistics services under one roof The facility will support road transport, air and ocean freight forwarding, warehousing and specialised delivery services. It will include 3,500 sqm for road transport operations and 3,000 sqm for Transport Related Warehousing, with space for approximately 3,000 pallets. Another 2,000 sqm will be dedicated to Special Delivery services, while 500 sqm will support the handling of dangerous goods under ADR requirements. The site will also feature more than 30 loading bays, office space and charging facilities for electric forklifts. Rhenus will transfer operations from its existing warehouses in Corso Spagna and Via Settima Strada. The move will take place gradually to maintain service continuity. Strengthening connections across Europe Interporto Padova provides access to major European transport routes, including the Mediterranean and Baltic-Adriatic corridors. The logistics centre also benefits from road and rail connections, with access to the A4 and A13 motorways and links to Venice and Verona airports. “With this hub, we are building on an established presence in the area and bringing different areas of expertise from the Rhenus Group under one roof,” said Guglielmo Davide Tassone, Managing Director of Rhenus Overland Italy. The new facility will strengthen Rhenus’ operations in north-eastern Italy and support the coordination of warehouse activities with national and international transport services. The company expects the integrated hub to improve the management of freight flows while providing additional space for future operations.

File Photo: Port of Long Beach Three senior House Republicans are calling on the Department of Homeland Security to revoke special inspection privileges granted to vessels operated by Chinese state-owned shipping giant COSCO, citing allegations that the company’s ships have been used to collect intelligence near U.S. coastlines. In an October 14 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford and Rep. Carlos Gimenez, chairman of the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security, called for COSCO vessels to be removed from the U.S. Coast Guard’s Qualship 21 program. The program rewards foreign-flagged vessels with strong safety and compliance records by allowing them to undergo fewer routine port state control inspections at U.S. ports. According to the lawmakers, at least 10 COSCO vessels were enrolled in the program as of July 15, despite the company’s designation by the Pentagon as a Chinese military company. An accompanying Coast Guard table identifies 11 vessels, including COSCO DEVELOPMENT , COSCO PRIDE and COSCO VIETNAM . The letter, which has now prompted a Coast Guard review, follows a September 1 Reuters investigation in which two senior Trump administration officials alleged that COSCO uses concealed equipment aboard its commercial ships to intercept military communications near the coastlines of the United States and other countries. The officials said the alleged intelligence-gathering operations were part of a decades-long relationship between COSCO and Beijing, allowing China to collect communications signals from ships and aircraft operating across Europe, North America and Asia. COSCO denied the allegations in a September statement, saying its onboard equipment serves legitimate commercial purposes, including navigation, communications and emergency response, and is not used for intelligence gathering or military surveillance. China’s embassy in Washington also rejected the allegations. The lawmakers argue that the reported activities warrant a review of whether COSCO should continue receiving preferential treatment under the Coast Guard program. “State-owned commercial vessels engaging in espionage is an expected breach of trust we regularly anticipate from the Chinese Communist Party,” the lawmakers wrote. They called on DHS to revoke COSCO vessels’ enrollment, refuse renewals and increase scrutiny of other companies suspected of conducting activities on behalf of China’s People’s Liberation Army. Beyond removing COSCO from Qualship 21, the lawmakers are seeking answers about what the Coast Guard knew about the alleged surveillance activities and when that information became available. They specifically asked whether Coast Guard Intelligence received warnings about COSCO from the Pentagon, intelligence agencies or other federal authorities before the September 1 Reuters report, and whether that information was considered when determining the vessels’ eligibility. In a statement to gCaptain, a Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed that on October 15, the Commandant has directed an immediate review of the vessels’ participation. “The U.S. Coast Guard is responsible for the safety and security of U.S. ports, waterways, and shipping, which are vital to our nation’s economic prosperity and national security. Every day, the Coast Guard takes decisive action to identify, mitigate, and address safety and security risks to our ports in the physical domain and cyberspace.” The lawmakers also questioned whether COSCO’s designation under Section 1260H, which identifies Chinese military companies operating in the United States, prompted a review of the company’s Qualship 21 status. Other questions concern whether the Coast Guard has conducted additional boardings of COSCO ships, whether it has sufficient authority to investigate suspected surveillance activities in U.S. waters, and whether analysts are examining historical vessel movements in the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone for patterns that could indicate intelligence collection. The letter also calls for a review of Hong Kong’s continued eligibility as a qualified flag administration under Qualship 21, citing concerns about Beijing’s control over the territory. The Coast Guard updated its Qualship 21 eligibility criteria earlier this year, expanding the circumstances under which vessels can be removed from the program, including certain associations with sanctioned entities and companies facing federal criminal investigations. “The U.S. Coast Guard continuously evaluates and updates its programs to address the dynamic and evolving security and safety landscape of the maritime industry,” the Coast Guard told gCaptain. “ The congressional request raises a separate question of whether national security intelligence and military-company designations should factor into decisions about which foreign vessels qualify for reduced inspections. Qualship 21 enrollment does not exempt vessels from security inspections or other Coast Guard enforcement actions, and the lawmakers’ request does not itself revoke COSCO’s eligibility. The Department of Homeland Security has not publicly announced any action in response to the letter. articles.summary: The International Energy Agency (IEA) has agreed to accelerate the release of approximately 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as the...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Shutterstock/Igor Grochev The International Energy Agency (IEA) has agreed to accelerate the release of approximately 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as the prolonged Strait of Hormuz crisis continues to strain global energy supplies. The decision, announced Thursday following a meeting of the agency’s Governing Board, comes amid mounting concerns over diesel shortages, high fuel prices and renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Middle East. According to the IEA’s statement , member countries have already released approximately 330 million barrels under the emergency stock release agreed in March in response to the Iran war. The agency said it would take steps to accelerate the remaining releases, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to be made available as soon as possible. The original agreement called for a record 400 million barrels of oil and petroleum products. However, some member countries have released more than initially pledged, while others plan to do the same, meaning the final total is expected to exceed 400 million barrels. The latest decision primarily speeds up previously committed releases rather than establishing an entirely new emergency stock drawdown. The IEA did not provide a specific timetable for completing the releases. The renewed push comes as the agency warns that the global diesel shortage could persist well into 2027. In its October Oil Market Report , published Wednesday, the IEA said disruptions to production and exports from the Middle East and Russia removed approximately 1.3 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil exports from the market in September compared with a year earlier. While crude oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have recovered significantly from their lows earlier in the conflict, refined petroleum product exports remain severely constrained. Middle Eastern refined product shipments averaged 1.9 million barrels per day in September, compared with 4.7 million barrels per day before the war. Meanwhile, total oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz reached 10.9 million barrels per day during September, supported by increased tanker movements and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Attacks on commercial vessels have intensified in October, including the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride after it was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The continued disruption is also eroding global oil inventories. The IEA estimates that observed oil stocks at the end of September were 509 million barrels below their pre-war levels, leaving the market with reduced protection against further supply shocks. Despite a rebound in Gulf crude exports, the agency expects constrained diesel supplies and elevated transportation costs to continue weighing on global energy markets. It forecasts global oil demand will decline by 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026 as higher prices and weaker economic activity take their toll. The Governing Board also called on member countries with oil production and refining capacity to increase supplies, particularly diesel, and emphasized the importance of maintaining the free flow of energy trade. The IEA said it would continue monitoring the emergency releases and provide further recommendations to G7 leaders based on updated market assessments, with particular attention to diesel supplies. articles.title: All American Marine Build Report: October 2026
articles.summary: All American Marine recently launched M/V North Star, the second high-speed, long-range eco-tour vessel built for Phillips Cruises & Tours. Like her sistership, Chugach Express, North Star will operate from Whittier, Alaska, carrying passengers…
articles.body: All American Marine Build Report: October 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Ron Wille, President, All American Marine October 16, 2026 Credit: AAM All American Marine recently launched M/V North Star, the second high-speed, long-range eco-tour vessel built for Phillips Cruises & Tours. Like her sistership, Chugach Express, North Star will operate from Whittier, Alaska, carrying passengers through the tidewater glaciers and wildlife-filled waters of Prince William Sound. The 84.5-foot, hydrofoil-assisted aluminum catamaran features a Teknicraft Design semi-displacement hull and is certified to USCG Subchapter T standards for up to 150 passengers. Her propulsion package mirrors that of Chugach Express: four MJP 350X waterjets driven by quad 800 mhp Scania DI16 082M engines, paired with Teknicraft’s dynamic hydrofoil system and wave-piercing bow. A repeat order is performance data in its clearest form. After operating Chugach Express through three demanding Alaska seasons, with full passenger loads, long days, and changing conditions. Phillips knew this platform could deliver. One of the most notable changes is fuel capacity with Chugach Express carrying 1,200 gallons, while North Star carries 1,600. The increase did not require a redesign; it was made possible by proven performance. Chugach Express demonstrated that the hull could carry additional weight without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or ride quality. The second vessel uses that margin to add 400 gallons and extend its operating range. But range is only part of the story. The Teknicraft hull and dynamic hydrofoil system are designed to reduce vessel accelerations underway, while the hull form and foil provide added motion damping at rest. For passengers, that means a more comfortable ride. For operators, it means a broader usable weather window, supporting more operating days, greater schedule reliability, and stronger revenue potential. That capability matters in Prince William Sound. Maintaining comfortable speeds in changing sea conditions can preserve more time at the destination while keeping the return schedule within reach. It can also mean the difference between completing a tour and remaining at the dock. Last month, we examined how little fuel consumption changes between light and fully loaded conditions on a Teknicraft hull. North Star shows what an operator can do with that margin. Greater fuel capacity, strong seakeeping, and efficient performance combine to create something more valuable than any single specification: greater operating capacity. WHAT OPERATORS ARE ASKING Top speed tells only part of the story. Passenger vessel operators need to know how a vessel rides at full load in real conditions, how guests feel after five or six hours aboard, and how much of the schedule can be maintained when the weather turns. Those are seakeeping questions, and on a tour vessel, they show up in two places. The first is underway. During transit, the Teknicraft hull form and hydrofoil lift work together to reduce vertical accelerations, the pounding and slamming that wear on passengers and crew over a long day. The second is on scene. At a glacier’s face or alongside a pod of humpbacks, low-speed motion is often when passengers begin to feel unwell. Here, the hull form and foil help dampen that motion. Guests stay on deck, crews remain ready to work, and fewer people become what one of our operators calls “mal de mer zombies.” One additional advantage comes in the adjustable hydrofoil. By de-tuning it, captains can make the vessel ride “heavier” at wildlife-viewing speeds, settling the hull and creating a steadier viewing platform. The vessel remains light and fuel-efficient during transit, then becomes more planted once on scene. Weather is where seakeeping becomes operating capacity. These hulls can maintain comfortable speeds in conditions that force other vessels to slow down or remain at the dock. That broader operating window supports more completed trips, greater schedule reliability, and stronger revenue potential. WHAT IT SIGNALS As Alaska’s tour season winds down, passenger vessel operators head into the off-season with a full season of results in hand. That is when a vessel should be evaluated, by what it delivered through months of real service. What these operators have learned is straightforward: comfort is operating capacity. A vessel that can sail comfortably in more conditions completes more departures, issues fewer refunds, and protects revenue. A vessel that remains steady at low speed keeps guests on deck and engaged. A hull with additional carrying capacity gives operators options, and Phillips Cruises and Tours chose to turn that margin into greater range. Real performance is measured across the entire operating day: at full load, through a full season, and in the weather operators encounter, not the weather they started the season wishing for.

articles.body: Incat Crowther to Build Fourth Fast Support Intervention Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Incat Crowther Zamil Offshore commissioned Incat Crowther and Singaporean shipbuilder Lita Ocean to design, build and deliver a fourth 60-m ABS-classed monohull Fast Support Intervention Vessel (FSIV). The project follows the delivery of the third vessel in the original fleet with the performance of the fleet leading to the order of a fourth vessel. The FSIV fleet is assisting Zamil Offshore with the efficient and safe transport of cargo, heavy maintenance equipment and personnel for Saudi Aramco’s operations in the Arabian Sea. Capable of speeds up to 36 knots, the vessels are powered by four MTU 16V4000 diesel engines coupled to ZF gearboxes driving Hamilton HT810 waterjets . Maneuverability of the DP2-certified vessels is enhanced by three Hydromaster tunnel bow thrusters , allowing safe docking and offshore station-keeping for transfer of cargo and personnel. Two of the main engines are coupled to FFS firefighting pumps paired with 1200 cu. m./hr. water monitors and shipboard water spray protection offering FiFi-1 capability. Three Scania 300kW diesel generators provide ship service power. The main deck offers an expansive 250 sq. m. aft cargo deck rated at 2.5 t/ m2 along with an optional Palfinger PK12000M deck crane . A climate-controlled forward cabin features business-class seating for 56 service personnel, as well as two bathrooms, a 15 sq. m. workshop, a 15 sq. m. storage room, a lounge and snack bar. The crew of 20 on the vessel are housed on the hull deck which features a large pantry, mess, three bathrooms and two laundry rooms. The vessels comply with the latest MCVSR requirements from Saudi Aramco, including ABS SMART notation . Construction is now underway on the fourth vessel, with the vessel set to join its predecessors in service by 2027.

articles.body: The DynaLiners Shares Index rebounded during the latest trading week, gaining 75 points, or 2.8%, to move above the 2,800-point threshold and reach its highest level of 2026. The recovery came despite continued pressure on global trade and economic activity, with container shipping companies providing the strongest support to the overall index. The DLSI Carriers index climbed 199 points, or 5.1%, to close at 4,081. The result represented another 2026 high and returned the carrier segment to its position as the leading sector index. The remaining sector indices recorded only marginal movements, ranging from a 0.3% decline for DLSI Ports to gains of up to 0.5%. Across the companies tracked by DynaLiners, 67 recorded share-price increases, compared with 51 declines. The average weekly gain stood at 1.9%, although this figure was heavily influenced by Mercantile Ports & Logistics, whose share price surged by 169%. DynaLiners noted that the company’s volatility reflects its low absolute share price, equivalent to approximately US$0.05 even after the increase. Excluding this movement, the average weekly change would have been 0.5%. Carrier stocks dominated the strongest performers. Of the next 15 largest weekly gainers, 13 were container shipping companies, led by Orient Overseas International Limited with a 16% increase. At the opposite end of the ranking, shipowner Seacon declined by 14%, while Vietnam Maritime Corporation recorded the largest loss, falling by 19%.

The transaction was finalised following approval from the relevant authorities. articles.summary: Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia conducted a ground deployment exercise (GDX) under the Revolving Fund Committee to strengthen coordination in responding to oil spills in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Conducted ahead of Singapore’s 17th Joint Oil Spill Exercise (JOSE) 2026…
articles.body: Singapore Conducts Oil Spill Response Drill Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia conducted a ground deployment exercise (GDX) under the Revolving Fund Committee to strengthen coordination in responding to oil spills in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Conducted ahead of Singapore’s 17th Joint Oil Spill Exercise (JOSE) 2026, the GDX simulated an oil spill originating from a vessel collision in Singapore waters, with the oil subsequently reaching the shores of Indonesia and Malaysia. Led by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the GDX tested information sharing, response planning and mutual assistance among the three littoral States. As part of the exercise, Indonesia and Malaysia deployed response assets in their respective waters to test their response arrangements under the exercise scenario. Separately, MPA hosted representatives from government agencies, industry partners and international organisations at the Integrated Operations Hub (IOH) Lab at ALICE@Mediapolis as part of JOSE 2026. The program provided an opportunity to share Singapore’s oil spill response capabilities and explore how emerging technologies could support future response operations. Representatives from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), ITOPF[1], Indonesia’s Directorate General of Sea Transportation and Malaysia’s Department of Environment also attended the program. Participants were briefed on the coordinated deployment of response assets for oil containment, dispersal and recovery, drawing on demonstrations conducted at sea. The program also highlighted how emerging technologies could enhance oil spill response. These included MPA’s Maritime Digital Twin (MDT), which uses modelling to predict the movement of spilled oil and identify potentially affected areas, as well as artificial intelligence to support response planning and resource deployment. Participants were also briefed on potential concepts of operations involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned surface vessels (USVs), including those trialled with ST Engineering. Drawing on demonstrations conducted at sea, the briefing illustrated how aerial surveillance could guide USVs in carrying out tasks such as dispersant spraying and oil containment boom towing. Overall, JOSE explored how such concepts of operations could be supported as unmanned technologies mature, potentially expanding the range of capabilities available for future oil spill response operations.

articles.summary: Steerprop was selected to supply its next-generation contra-rotating propeller (CRP) technology for Estonia's first fully electric passenger ferry, currently under construction at Poland's CRIST SA shipyard.The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet…
articles.body: Estonia's First Electric Ferry Takes Shape in Poland Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet, will feature two Steerprop SP 25 CRP units equipped with permanent magnet motors. Image courtesy Steerprop Steerprop was selected to supply its next-generation contra-rotating propeller (CRP) technology for Estonia's first fully electric passenger ferry, currently under construction at Poland's CRIST SA shipyard. The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet , will feature two Steerprop SP 25 CRP units equipped with permanent magnet motors. The propulsion system is designed to deliver high thrust and improved efficiency in both open water and ice conditions. Steerprop's CRP configuration uses two contra-rotating propellers on a single shaftline, allowing greater thrust and efficiency than comparable single-propeller arrangements. The latest generation introduces pressure lubrication, replacing immersion lubrication to reduce mechanical losses and improve mechanical efficiency by approximately 3.5 percentage points. "The latest Steerprop CRP development has resulted in a propulsor with unique efficiency and thrust performance, and one that offers an even greater performance boost for vessels operating in ice conditions," said Markku Miinala, Steerprop's Cruise & Ferry Segment Director. The ferry will incorporate a 3 MWh battery system charged using renewable shore power, supplemented by biodiesel generators for severe weather and emergency operations. Designed to 1B Ice Class requirements, the vessel will be capable of operating in ice up to 60 centimeters thick. Steerprop already supplies propulsion systems for four double-ended ferries operating on Estonia's Saaremaa and Hiiumaa routes. The propulsion equipment is scheduled for delivery in late 2027, with the ferry expected to enter service in late 2028. The vessel's design and construction contract is valued at €49.93 million, including €28 million in funding from the European Union Modernization Fund, with additional financing from Estonia's CO₂ quota trading mechanisms. October 16, 2026 The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, built by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding, features a WinGD dual-fuel ammonia engine and a Sun Rui Ammonia Fuel Supply System. Image courtesy Anglo Eastern Anglo-Eastern has detailed its role in developing and preparing CMB.TECH's Mineral Europa, the world's first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, which recently embarked on its maiden voyage. The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, built by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding, features a WinGD dual-fuel ammonia engine and a Sun Rui Ammonia Fuel Supply System. The vessel can operate on ammonia or conventional marine fuel, providing flexibility as ammonia bunkering infrastructure develops. Anglo-Eastern's involvement dates to 2018, when its technical services division began evaluating alternative fuels with CMB.TECH, initially examining hydrogen before progressing to ammonia. By 2020, Anglo-Eastern Technical Services (AETS) was developing the vessel's safety philosophy, fuel arrangements and preliminary engineering. The design received Approvals in Principle from Lloyd's Register and ABS in 2021. A central engineering challenge was integrating ammonia storage, double-wall piping, ventilation, leak detection, containment and emergency shutdown systems without sacrificing cargo capacity. "The technical challenge was not just accommodating a new fuel. Safety, containment and operational requirements all had to work together as an integrated system without compromising the vessel's primary purpose as a commercial cargo carrier," said Arunava Sengupta, Managing Director of AETS. Anglo-Eastern also supported newbuilding supervision, technical management and crew preparation. Vessel-specific operating, bunkering, maintenance and emergency procedures were developed alongside training incorporating a three-dimensional digital twin, fuel supply simulator and emergency scenarios. Senior officers participated in shipyard and sea trials. "Mineral Europa demonstrates what can be achieved when an owner's conviction is matched by deep engineering and operational capability," said Bjorn Hojgaard, Anglo-Eastern CEO. CMB.TECH CEO Alexander Saverys described the vessel's entry into service as a milestone in the company's decarbonization strategy, with additional ammonia-powered vessels expected to follow. Anglo-Eastern said it remains fuel-agnostic, supporting shipowners in evaluating alternative propulsion technologies according to their operational requirements. Image courtesy Anglo Eastern

articles.summary: Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
